scenes.name: Reggae roots y dub
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Junto al funk, la otra gran lección rítmica del postpunk: el bajo como protagonista, el espacio y el eco de la producción dub. Las técnicas de estudio de Jamaica (King Tubby, Lee Perry) se convierten en herramienta de vanguardia para PiL, The Slits, The Pop Group y On-U Sound.
scenes.family: Ritmos negros: dub, funk, disco y hip hop

podcast.title: Departure from The Wailers (1973)
podcast.body: Peter Tosh left The Wailers in 1973, citing unhappiness with Chris Blackwell's refusal to support his solo work and a perception that Bob Marley, being lighter-skinned, received preferential attention within the band and from the label. "Tosh left the wailers in 1973. He was unhappy that Chris Blackwell would not let him put out a solo album and there were rumblings about the attention going to Marley."

podcast.title: Bitterness Over Marley's Skin Tone
podcast.body: Part of Peter Tosh's resentment stemmed from his belief that Bob Marley garnered more attention due to his lighter skin, leading Tosh to fundamentally align himself with the "black camp" amidst Jamaica's societal dynamics, as described by author Colin Grant. "Some of that bitterness was from Tosh's point of view due to Marley being lighter skinned than he was."

podcast.title: Inspiration for 2 Tone Mascot
podcast.body: An old photograph of reggae star Peter Tosh served as the direct inspiration for the black and white rude boy image created by Jerry Dammers. This image later became known as Walt Japsco, the unofficial mascot of Dammers' 2 Tone record label and the broader Ska movement. "In fact, it was based on a photo, a very old picture of reggae star Peter Tosh."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for The Specials' Logo
podcast.body: Peter Tosh, a Jamaican musician and former member of Bob Marley's Wailers, was the real-life individual whose photograph inspired the stylized Jamaican rude boy character, Walt Japsco, featured in The Specials' band logo. "Walt was actually based on a photograph of Jamaican musician Peter Tosh, who was a former member of Bob Arley's Whalers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marijuana Dealer Funding
podcast.body: After Chris Blackwell declined to fund his solo album, Peter Tosh secured the necessary money for "Legalize It" from a marijuana dealer, who initially expressed displeasure with the album's controversial title. "Since Chris Blackwell would not fund his solo album, Tosh got a marijuana dealer to give him the money for legalize it, although the dealer initially was not too happy about the name of the album."

podcast.title: Newspaper Ad for "Legalize It"
podcast.body: In response to the Jamaican government's attempt to ban his record, Peter Tosh took a defiant stance by purchasing an advertisement in a Jamaican newspaper to print the complete lyrics of "Legalize It," ensuring his message reached the public. "Tosh also took out an ad and a Jamaican newspaper and printed the lyrics within the ad."

podcast.title: Political Activism
podcast.body: Peter Tosh was a fervent political activist who personally endured police brutality, and his protests were profoundly influenced by the works of American civil rights leaders such as Dr. Martin Luther King, Stokely Carmichael, and Malcolm X, even though their writings were banned in Jamaica. "He did not just protest police brutality because of articles he read. He experienced it firsthand."

xref.title: Two-Tone Records Founded 1979 – Black-and-White Logo Based on Peter Tosh Photo; Anti-Racist Mission
xref.body: Jerry Dammers founded Two-Tone Records, naming it after the black-and-white suits worn by mods and skinheads of the 1960s and after the peaceful multiracial makeup of the band. The label's logo — a man in a black and white suit, white shirt, black tie, sunglasses, pork pie hat, white socks, and black loafers — was drawn by Dammers based on a photo of Peter Tosh when he was a member of the Wailers. The character was named Walt Jabsco (Walt after Walt Disney). Two-Tone had an explicit anti-racism message at a time when racial tensions in the UK were getting out of control. "Two-tone became the core of the second wave of Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
